Diode. A two-terminal semiconductor device constructed from a PN junction—p-type and n-type silicon fused together—that conducts current primarily in one direction. Diodes are the foundation for rectification, protection, and non-linear circuit functions, allowing current to flow when forward-biased and blocking it when reverse-biased.

Forward bias means positive voltage is applied to the p-side, which enables current flow across the junction. Reverse bias applies negative voltage to the p-side and blocks current, except for a small leakage current. The forward voltage drop across a silicon diode is roughly zero point seven volts, while for germanium it is around zero point three volts. This constant drop defines rectified and clamping circuits. A diode conducts when the forward voltage exceeds its threshold—zero point seven volts for silicon. Below that threshold, the junction capacitance stores charge but negligible current flows.

Reverse breakdown occurs at the reverse voltage rating, for example one thousand volts for a common 1N4007 diode. Exceeding this rating causes avalanche multiplication and device failure, which is destructive unless the current is limited.

Schottky diodes use a metal-semiconductor junction instead of a PN junction, giving them a lower forward drop of roughly zero point three to zero point four volts for silicon, with even lower values possible. They also switch faster, which is critical in switching power supplies. The PIN diode has an intrinsic, undoped layer that provides high impedance during reverse bias and acts as a voltage-dependent resistor for RF switching. The Zener diode operates in reverse breakdown with a stable knee voltage and is used as a voltage regulator and protection device. The Varactor diode's capacitance varies with reverse voltage, making it useful for frequency tuning and phase modulators.
